mcqs.question: Why do interviewers sometimes deliberately withhold a requested number or requirement, even after being asked directly?
options: To penalize candidates who ask too many questions
To simulate the realistic condition of incomplete specs and see whether the candidate can still make defensible progress
Because they genuinely don't know the answer themselves
To reduce the total number of topics covered in the interview
mcqs.explanation: Withholding information on purpose simulates real engineering ambiguity — the test is whether you can proceed with a reasonable, stated assumption. It isn't a penalty for asking, and it isn't about the interviewer's own knowledge or trimming interview scope.

mcqs.question: After asking about scale two or three times and getting "whatever you think is reasonable" each time, what's the best next move?
options: Ask a fourth time with different phrasing until a number is given
Design the system without ever assuming a scale
State your own number with a brief reason, and proceed while flagging where it matters most
End the requirements phase and move directly to wrap-up
mcqs.explanation: Once repeated rephrasing hasn't produced a number, stating your own reasoned assumption and moving forward is the productive path — asking again mostly burns time, and designing with no scale assumption at all isn't realistic. Skipping to wrap-up abandons the rest of the interview.

mcqs.question: What's the main advantage of narrating an assumption out loud instead of silently guessing and continuing?
options: It makes the interview last exactly the allotted time
It guarantees the assumption is correct
It is required by most interview scoring rubrics
It lets the interviewer confirm or redirect the assumption immediately, instead of a wrong guess surfacing only much later
mcqs.explanation: Narrating the assumption gives the interviewer a chance to correct it right away, keeping the cost of being wrong low — silent guessing hides the same risk until it surfaces as a contradiction later. It doesn't guarantee correctness or control interview length, and it isn't a formal rubric requirement.

mcqs.question: A candidate repeats "I need more information to proceed" several times when the interviewer won't give a specific number. How does this typically read?
options: As an inability to operate under realistic uncertainty, which is the opposite of what's being tested
As a neutral, safe default with no real downside
As a sign the interviewer's question was unfair
mcqs.explanation: Repeatedly stalling on an unanswered question signals the opposite of the skill being probed — the stronger move is a stated, defensible assumption. It isn't neutral, isn't inherently rigorous, and doesn't reflect on the fairness of the question.
